title: How Do You Set Alert Thresholds for Emerging Customer Feedback Issues Without Drowning in False Alarms?
summary: Set feedback alert thresholds on change against each theme's own baseline, add a minimum volume floor, and agree who acts before an alert fires.
body_markdown:
Most feedback alerts fail in one of two ways. Set the threshold low and the inbox fills with spikes that turn out to be noise, so people stop reading. Set it high and the real issue only trips the alert once it's already big. Either way, the alert stops doing its job.


The fix is to change what the threshold measures. Set alert thresholds on change against each theme's own baseline, not on raw counts. Add a minimum volume floor so small themes can't trip an alert on a handful of comments. Then decide, before any alert fires, who acts on it and by when. That combination cuts false alarms without hiding real emerging issues. Thematic's Spike Detection alerts work this way. They flag a theme when its volume or sentiment moves two standard deviations from its recent average. The alert goes to email or Slack on a daily, weekly or monthly schedule.


Below are the six steps, a worked example, and the mistakes that cause alert fatigue.


## The 6-step process


1. **Baseline each theme against itself.** Compare this period with the theme's own recent history, not with a fixed count.
2. **Set a minimum volume floor.** Don't let a statistical spike alert fire on a theme with too few comments to measure.
3. **Allow for testing many themes at once.** Watching hundreds of themes guarantees some chance alerts every cycle.
4. **Run separate lanes for spikes, new themes and tripwires.** Each kind of issue needs a different rule.
5. **Agree the owner and the response before the alert fires.** An alert nobody owns gets ignored.
6. **Review the alerts every month and retire the noisy ones.** Track how many alerts led to action.


## Step 1: Baseline each theme against itself


A raw-count threshold ("alert me when billing complaints pass 50 a week") treats every theme as if it had the same normal level. It doesn't. A noisy theme crosses a fixed line every few weeks for no reason. A quiet theme can triple and never reach it.


The better rule is the one behind statistical process control. The[NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pmc/section3/pmc32.htm) describes a control chart as one that "compares" the current performance of the process to the past performance. Applied to feedback, each theme gets its own expected range, built from its own recent periods. An alert fires only when the theme moves outside that range.


Thematic's[Significant Changes](https://help.getthematic.com/article/76-significant-changes-explination) view uses this approach. It looks at each theme's last six periods and flags themes whose volume or score is more than two standard deviations from their recent average. It then filters for statistical significance (p<0.05) and ranks themes by the size of the change.


Track volume and sentiment as separate signals. A theme can hold steady in volume while getting angrier, and that's a different problem from a theme that suddenly doubles.


## Step 2: Set a minimum volume floor


Percentages mislead when the base is small. A theme that goes from three comments to six has doubled, but nothing has necessarily changed.


The statistics explain why. For a proportion, the NIST control limits are p ± 3·√(p(1−p)/n), where n is the number of responses in the period ([NIST p-chart](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pmc/section3/pmc332.htm) ). The band is wide when n is small and narrow when n is large. As an illustration, take a theme that normally makes up 2% of comments:


Responses per week Expected range for a 2% theme (3-sigma)


500 0.1% to 3.9%


5,000 1.4% to 2.6%


At 500 responses a week, a theme can nearly double by chance. So set a floor below which a theme doesn't get a statistical spike alert, and size it from your weekly volume. If most themes sit under the floor, move to a weekly or monthly comparison window so each period carries more comments.


A floor is a filter for spike alerts. It isn't a rule to wait before acting. Small but growing issues are caught by the separate lane in Step 4. For how sample size affects theme reliability, see[How many customer feedback responses do you need before AI themes are reliable?](https://getthematic.com/insights/responses-needed-ai-themes-reliable) .


## Step 3: Allow for testing many themes at once


A feedback program with 200 themes runs 200 tests every cycle. At a 5% significance level, about 10 of those themes could look significant by chance alone, even when nothing has changed.


Statisticians call this the multiple comparisons problem.[Benjamini and Hochberg (1995)](https://www.dcscience.net/Benjamini-Hochberg-1995-FDR.pdf) put it plainly: "An unguarded use of single-inference procedures results in a greatly increased false positive (significance) rate." Their answer, controlling the false discovery rate, limits the share of flagged results that are false.


In practice, analysts have three options:


- **Use a stricter threshold** for themes that matter less, and keep the default for the themes you track closely.
- **Require the change to hold for two periods** before alerting on low-priority themes.
- **Rank flagged themes by the size of the change** , so the biggest moves get read first.


## Step 4: Run separate lanes for spikes, new themes and tripwires


One rule can't catch every kind of issue. Use three lanes, each with its own trigger:


Lane Catches Trigger Thematic feature


Spikes An existing theme that jumps or drops Change against the theme's own baseline Spike Detection workflow


New and rare themes Issues too small or too new to have a baseline A new theme appears, or a small theme keeps rising Theme Discovery workflow; rare themes in Significant Changes


Tripwires High-severity terms where one comment is enough Any comment matching a keyword or filter Comment Matching workflow


Thematic's Spike Detection flags changes of two standard deviations from the recent average. Apply your volume floor and stricter thresholds from Steps 2 and 3 when you triage what it flags. The tripwire lane has no volume floor at all. If a comment mentions a safety issue, a data breach or legal action, someone should read it the same day. Scope each lane with filters too. Thematic's Spike Detection can watch, for example, theme volume among detractors only, or by location.


The[six approaches to detecting emerging customer issues](https://getthematic.com/insights/detect-emerging-customer-issues-approaches) compares these methods in more depth.


## Step 5: Agree the owner and the response before the alert fires


An alert is only useful if someone acts on it. Google's[Site Reliability Engineering book](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/) sets the standard: "Every page should be actionable." It also warns that "When pages occur too frequently, employees second-guess, skim, or even ignore incoming alerts."


For each alert, agree three things in advance:


- **The owner.** One named team per theme family (billing, delivery, app), plus a backup.
- **The first response.** Read the comments behind the spike, check which segment moved, size the impact and[route it](https://getthematic.com/insights/automated-customer-insights-routing) .[Spotting emerging support issues](https://getthematic.com/insights/spot-emerging-support-issues-customer-feedback) covers this triage in detail.
- **What "no action" means.** If the owner decides the spike is noise, they record why. That note feeds Step 6.


Send each alert to the channel the owner already works in.[Thematic workflows](https://getthematic.com/insights/product-update-workflows) deliver to email or Slack.


## Step 6: Review the alerts every month and retire the noisy ones


Thresholds drift out of date as feedback volume and themes change. Once a month, count the alerts each rule sent and how many led to action. That ratio is your alert precision.


- **Low precision:** raise the floor, lengthen the comparison window, or move the theme to a stricter threshold.
- **Never fires:** the Google SRE book suggests that alerting exercised "less than once a quarter for some SRE teams" should be up for removal.
- **Missed a real issue:** lower the floor for that theme, or add a tripwire.


Before treating any spike as real, check it against the same period last year.[Real trend or seasonal?](https://getthematic.com/insights/real-trend-or-seasonal-customer-feedback) explains how.


## What does this look like in practice?


Greyhound, the bus network serving the United States, Canada and Mexico, ran a post-trip customer survey for years. The team used to compile results by hand, and by the time a report was ready the data was already three to four weeks old.


After moving to Thematic, Greyhound's station managers checked their dashboards once or twice a week for new themes. When a cleaning issue appeared at the Dallas terminal, Greyhound's team said that "Thematic pointed it out to us within 2 minutes." The issue reached the person who could fix it, the station manager, without waiting for a monthly report.


The lesson for thresholds: the detection only mattered because the owner was already agreed. The station manager knew the Dallas terminal was theirs.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Alerting on raw counts.** Use change against each theme's own baseline instead.
- **Treating percentage jumps on tiny themes as signal.** Apply a volume floor to spike alerts.
- **Ignoring how many themes you test.** Expect chance alerts every cycle and use stricter rules for lower-priority themes.
- **Using one rule for everything.** Run spikes, new themes and tripwires as separate lanes.
- **Sending alerts to a shared inbox.** Name an owner and a first response for every alert.
- **Never tuning the thresholds.** Review alert precision monthly and retire rules that never lead to action.
- **Confusing seasonal patterns with spikes.** Compare against the same period last year before escalating.
